questions.text: In CLIP training, what does the symmetric contrastive objective encourage?

options.A: Each image to match every caption in its training batch equally.
options.B: Paired images and captions to outrank mismatches in both directions.
options.C: Each image encoder to reconstruct its original pixels from captions.
options.D: Image and text embeddings to occupy unrelated representation spaces.

questions.explanation: Image-to-text and text-to-image cross-entropies both use paired examples as positives and other batch entries as negatives.

questions.text: You have a pretrained CLIP model and new class names, but no labeled training images. How do you perform zero-shot classification?

options.A: Train a new linear classifier using the class names as image labels.
options.B: Choose the class prompt with the smallest embedding vector norm.
options.C: Generate a caption and compare its character count with each class name.
options.D: Embed class prompts and select the highest cosine similarity to the image.

questions.explanation: Zero-shot classification compares the image embedding with text embeddings of candidate class prompts, without training a new classifier.

questions.text: What class ranks first for zero_shot_classify([2, 0], {"cat": [1, 1], "dog": [1, 0]}) in the lesson code?

options.A: dog, because its normalized vector has cosine similarity 1.
options.B: cat, because its unnormalized vector has the larger coordinate sum.
options.C: cat, because the function preserves dictionary insertion order.
options.D: dog, because the function chooses the smallest cosine similarity.

questions.explanation: The function normalizes image and class vectors, computes dot products, and sorts descending. Dog scores 1; cat scores 1/sqrt(2).
